title: Two views of allocating scarce places
bodyMd:
**Passage A**

When a public workshop has more eligible applicants than places and no relevant difference in need, a lottery is preferable to discretionary selection. A panel may sincerely believe it can recognize commitment from an application, yet polished prose often reflects access to advice rather than willingness to participate. A lottery acknowledges that the institution lacks a defensible basis for ranking otherwise eligible people. The panel's uncertainty is not itself a defect to conceal. An honest institution can admit that its evidence does not support a fine ranking among people who have met the relevant conditions. It may be tempting to retain discretion because selecting named winners feels more responsible than drawing lots. But responsibility also includes recognizing when a confident decision would exceed the available grounds. In such a case, randomness makes the limit visible and prevents a weak impression from acquiring the force of an official judgment about an applicant.

The procedure does not make losing pleasant, but it makes the reason for losing intelligible. Every eligible applicant faces the same chance, and the institution need not manufacture fine distinctions it cannot justify. The argument is limited: where applicants have substantially different needs or where a skill is essential to participation, eligibility or priority rules may legitimately differ. Random selection is a response to relevant equality, not a denial that relevant differences ever exist.

**Passage B**

Equal chances can conceal unequal ability to use a prize. Imagine a workshop that allocates places fairly but offers sessions only during standard working hours. A lottery may give a shift worker and a person with flexible employment the same chance of admission, while only one can reliably attend. The selection procedure is impartial at the moment of allocation, yet the programme remains unequal in practical access.

This does not justify returning to opaque panels. It calls for examining what happens before and after selection: how people learn of the programme, whether the application is accessible, and whether attendance requires unaffordable sacrifices. A lottery can be part of a fair system. It cannot by itself make the whole system fair, because randomness does not remove the obstacles that determine who enters the pool and who can benefit after winning.
